f.t: The Chakma make up more than half of the Indigenous population of Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts.
Regulations of 1900 confirmed that the Chittagong Hill Tracts were largely self-governing in internal matters.
Hill Tracts peoples are sometimes called Jumma, after jum, their traditional method of shifting cultivation.

n.l: Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh, and parts of northeast India

f.t: Together, the Chakma, Marma and Tripura make up about 90 percent of the Indigenous peoples of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

n.l: Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh

f.t: The Mru call themselves Marucha; in their language, maru means human.
The Mru alphabet, invented in the 1980s and unrelated to any other script, is encoded in the Unicode Standard with its own digits.
School textbooks up to class three have been published in the Mru language and alphabet.

n.l: Bandarban district in the Chittagong Hill Tracts of Bangladesh, and nearby areas of Myanmar

f.t: Tripura University opened a Department of Kokborok in 2015 and began doctoral research in the language in 2018.
Kokborok, the Tripura language, has been an official language of the Indian state of Tripura since 1979.
In Bangladesh, Tripura communities live in the Chittagong Hill Tracts and in districts such as Comilla, Chandpur, Moulvibazar and Dhaka.

n.l: Chittagong Hill Tracts and other districts of Bangladesh, and the state of Tripura, India

f.t: Dayak is a shared name for many Indigenous peoples of Borneo, by some estimates about 450 ethnolinguistic groups.
Dayak peoples share traditions of longhouse living and customary law known as adat.

n.l: Borneo: Kalimantan (Indonesia), Sabah and Sarawak (Malaysia) and Brunei

f.p: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme
f.t: On Siberut, a UNESCO biosphere reserve since 1981, Mentawai communities use the forest with care, guided by traditional knowledge.

f.p: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme
f.t: Siberut, home to many Mentawai communities, is the largest of the four Mentawai Islands west of Sumatra.

n.l: The Mentawai Islands, including Siberut, off West Sumatra, Indonesia

f.p: Prime Minister's Office, Government of India
f.t: India's government names the Bhil among the tribal peoples whose movements strengthened the country's freedom struggle.

n.l: Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra, India

f.p: Directorate of Information and Public Relations, Government of Assam
f.t: Bodo is an associate official language of Assam, and in 2022 the state announced it would become a medium of instruction in Classes XI and XII.

f.p: Directorate of Information and Public Relations, Government of Assam
f.t: The Bodo Sahitya Sabha, founded on 16 November 1952, has grown into an important body for promoting Bodo language and literature.

n.l: Bodoland Territorial Region and other parts of Assam, India

f.t: The Garo Hills Autonomous District Council, set up in 1952 under India's Sixth Schedule, is based in Tura and covers five districts.

f.p: Department of Arts and Culture, Government of Meghalaya
f.t: The Garo include 12 sub-groups, among them the Atong, Chibok, Me'gam and Chisak, who share a common language and culture.
The Meghalaya government lists Garo among the state's languages, alongside Khasi, Pnar and English.
Wangala, the Garo harvest festival also called the 100 drums festival, helps Garo people keep their cultural identity strong in Meghalaya.

n.l: Garo Hills of Meghalaya, India, and north-central Bangladesh

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: Odisha counted 888,581 Gond people in the 2011 census, and Gond communities live mainly in Madhya Pradesh.
Gond painting, mostly made in Patangarh village in Dindori district, gained worldwide recognition after shows in Tokyo and Paris and became a livelihood for many tribal families.
Masaram Gondi, a script created in 1918 by Munshi Mangal Singh Masaram of Madhya Pradesh to write the Gondi language, is still used today in handwritten and printed materials.

n.l: Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra, Telangana, Odisha and neighboring states of central India

f.p: Dr. Ramdayal Munda Tribal Welfare Research Institute, Jharkhand
f.t: The Ho call themselves Ho, Hodoko or Horo, words that mean human in their own language.

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: In Odisha, Ho farmers grow paddy, maize and ragi, tend kitchen gardens, and gather mushrooms, mahua and greens from the forest.
The Ho language has its own recently devised alphabet, Warang Citi, which is encoded in the Unicode Standard and used by a yearly and a biweekly publication.

n.l: Kolhan region of Jharkhand and northern Odisha, with communities in West Bengal and Bihar, India

f.t: The Khasi Hills Autonomous District Council has a wing that oversees the Elakas, the traditional Khasi states.
The Khasi Hills, home mainly to the Khasi, are now divided into five districts of Meghalaya.
Apart from Shillong's municipality and cantonment, all of Meghalaya is governed under the Sixth Schedule, the only northeast state where this is so.

n.l: Khasi Hills of Meghalaya, India, and nearby Bangladesh

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: Odisha counted 358,112 Kurukh (Oraon) people in 2011; many farm and practice crafts such as carpentry, rope making and weaving date palm leaf mats.
Kurukh has its own alphabet, Tolong Siki, created in 1988, officially recognized by Jharkhand in 2007 and now part of the Unicode Standard.

f.p: Dr. Ramdayal Munda Tribal Welfare Research Institute, Jharkhand
f.t: Twelve to thirty Kurukh villages join in a Parha council, where members of each village council meet under a Parha chief.

n.l: Jharkhand, Odisha, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal in India, with communities in Assam, Bangladesh and Nepal

f.t: Mizoram became a full state of India on 20 February 1987; its Legislative Assembly first met on 10 May 1972.
Historically, every Mizo village had its own chief, who was assisted by a council of elders.

f.p: Prime Minister's Office, Government of India
f.t: India's government names the Mizo among the tribal peoples whose movements strengthened the country's freedom struggle.

n.l: Mizoram, northeast India

f.t: Mundari has its own script, known in the community as Mundari Bani; a version reformed in 2008 by Munda community bodies is in the Unicode Standard.

f.p: Dr. Ramdayal Munda Tribal Welfare Research Institute, Jharkhand
f.t: Munda call their dance durang and their song susun, and both women and men dance at social events and seasonal festivals.

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: The Munda call themselves Hodoko, which means human in their own language, Mundari.

n.l: Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Bihar in India, with communities in Bangladesh

f.p: Nagaland State Portal, Government of Nagaland
f.t: Nagaland's state portal lists 17 major tribes living in the state, each with its own language and festivals.
Each December the Government of Nagaland hosts the Hornbill Festival near Kohima, where all the state's tribes share their cultures.

f.p: Nagaland State Portal, Government of Nagaland
f.t: Naga peoples pass on their history orally, in songs and fables and to the rhythm of log drums.

n.l: Nagaland, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh in India, and neighbouring Myanmar

f.t: On 25 December 2025, India's Constitution was released in the Santali language, written in the Ol Chiki script.

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: Odisha counted 894,764 Santal people in the 2011 census, most living in settled villages of 50 to 100 households.

f.p: Odisha State Tribal Museum (SCSTRTI, Government of Odisha)
f.t: Santal homes in Odisha are decorated with wall paintings of animals, people and flowers.

n.l: Jharkhand, West Bengal, Odisha and nearby states of India, northwest Bangladesh, and Nepal

f.p: Upopoy National Ainu Museum and Park
f.t: Upopoy, a national centre for Ainu history and culture in Shiraoi, Hokkaido, opened to the public in July 2020.

f.p: Japanese Law Translation, Ministry of Justice, Japan
f.t: A 2019 Japanese law names the Ainu as an Indigenous people of northern Japan, especially Hokkaido, and aims for a society that respects Ainu pride.
In the Ainu language, the word Ainu means human, and it is also the name of the people.

n.l: Hokkaido and other parts of Japan

f.t: In 1983, 51,468 hectares of Wanniyala-Aetto customary land were declared the Maduru Oya National Park.
Their own name, Wanniyala-Aetto, means forest dwellers, and their ancestors lived on the island long before the Sinhalese and the Tamils arrived.

n.l: Eastern Sri Lanka, including the Maduru Oya area

f.t: Karen communities have lived in what is now northern Thailand for many centuries.
Karen is a name for several related peoples who speak 12 related Karenic languages; about 85 percent of Karen belong to the S'gaw or Pwo branches.

n.l: Eastern Myanmar, including Karen State, and western and northern Thailand

f.t: In 2011 the Tun Jugah Foundation published Bup Sereba Reti Jaku Iban, described as the first monolingual Iban dictionary.
To keep Iban ikat weaving strong, weavers are urged to grow natural dye plants such as engkudu (morinda) and indigo.
Between 1948 and 1963 the Iban language served as the common language between Sarawak's communities.

n.l: Sarawak, Malaysia, with communities in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, and Brunei

f.t: The Kadazan Dusun Cultural Association, founded in 1966, represents 48 Indigenous ethnic communities of Sabah.
Each year the community celebrates Kaamatan, the harvest festival, which brings Sabah's peoples together.
KDCA works on preserving, standardizing and developing the Kadazandusun language with its many dialects.

n.l: Sabah, Malaysia

f.t: Orang Asli were collectors and primary traders in the peninsula's economy as early as the 5th century CE.
Orang Asli, a Malay collective term meaning original or first peoples, covers 18 officially listed groups of Peninsular Malaysia.
The Orang Asli are not one group: each people has its own language and culture and sees itself as distinct.
Some Temuan, Jakun and Semai families now run their own rubber, oil palm or cocoa farms.

n.l: Peninsular Malaysia

f.t: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Magar as an official language for both Gandaki and Karnali provinces.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Nepal's 2021 census counted 2,013,498 Magar people, living mostly in Lumbini, Gandaki and Bagmati provinces.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Magar communities keep customary institutions such as the bheja, and each year they choose a mukhiya as community leader, who settles small disputes.

n.l: Hills of the Rapti and Gandaki river basins in western and central Nepal, and communities across Nepal

f.t: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Nepal Bhasa, alongside Tamang, as an official language of Bagmati Province.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: The Newa homeland is the Kathmandu Valley, called Swanigah in Nepal Bhasa; in 2021 more than half of Nepal's 1,341,363 Newa lived in its three districts.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Nepal Bhasa, the Newa language, has its own scripts, Ranjana and Prachalit, along with its own grammar, dictionaries and literature.

n.l: Swanigah, the Kathmandu Valley (Kathmandu, Lalitpur and Bhaktapur), and towns across Nepal

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: The Rai homeland is Majh Kirat, also called Khambuwan, in the middle hills of eastern Nepal.
The Kirat Rai Yayokkha, founded in 1990, works to unite Nepal's diverse Rai communities and to promote Rai languages, arts and literature.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: The Rai are a multilingual people: the Kirat Rai Yayokkha has registered 26 Rai language groups, among them Bantawa, Chamling and Kulung.

n.l: Majh Kirat, also called Khambuwan, in the middle hills of eastern Nepal between the Dudh Koshi and Arun rivers, plus Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari and the Kathmandu Valley

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: In Nepal's 2021 census, 90.3 percent of Sherpa people reported Sherpa as their own language.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Sherpa communities use a customary system called nawa to look after crops and forests.
UNESCO describes conservation-minded Sherpa culture as the backbone of biodiversity conservation in the Khumbu region of Sagarmatha National Park.

n.l: Solukhumbu and the upper Dudh Koshi and Sun Koshi valleys of northeastern Nepal, from Solu to Helambu, and Kathmandu

f.t: Tamang is the mother tongue of about 4.88 percent of Nepal's population, according to the 2021 census.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: The Tamang are on the Nepal government's official list of Adivasi Janajati, or Indigenous nationalities.

n.l: Hills around the Kathmandu Valley and central Nepal

f.t: In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Gurung, the Tamu language, as an official language of Gandaki Province.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Tamu Kyui, the Tamu language, now has its own Khema script, which Nepal's Language Commission has recognized.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: Through the Rodhi, a Tamu tradition, young people learn social values, skills and knowledge from the older generation, with song and dance.

n.l: Tamuwan, the hills between the Trishuli and Kali Gandaki rivers in central Nepal, including Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Syangja, Manang and Mustang

f.t: Tharu is the mother tongue of about 5.88 percent of Nepal's population, according to the 2021 census.

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: The Tharu are on the Nepal government's official list of Adivasi Janajati, or Indigenous nationalities.

n.l: The Terai plains of southern Nepal, and neighbouring India

f.p: National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities, Nepal
f.t: In Nepal's 2021 census, 84.5 percent of Yakthung people reported Limbu as their mother tongue, a language with its own script, Sirijanga.
In 2021 Nepal's Language Commission recommended Limbu, alongside Maithili, as an official language of Province 1 in eastern Nepal.
Limbu, the Yakthung language, became an official language of Sikkim, India, in 1981, and its script is encoded in the Unicode Standard.

n.l: Limbuwan in the eastern hills of Nepal, including Taplejung, Panchthar, Terhathum and Ilam, plus Jhapa, Morang and Sunsari, with communities in Sikkim and Darjeeling, India

f.t: Benguet's official provincial fruit is a native blueberry whose Ibaloi name is ayosip.
Like their Kankanaey neighbours, Ibaloi farmers of Benguet have worked wet rice on terraced fields for centuries.
The Ibaloi are one of the three major ethnolinguistic groups of Benguet province, with the Kankanaey and Kalanguya.

n.l: Southern Benguet and the Baguio area in northern Luzon, Philippines

f.t: Ifugao families still farm and care for their mountain rice terraces, a UNESCO World Heritage living landscape since 1995.
The Hudhud, long narrative chants of the Ifugao sung at rice sowing and harvest, are on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.

n.l: Ifugao Province in the Cordillera mountains of northern Luzon, Philippines

f.t: Benguet's official provincial fruit is a native blueberry, known in Kankanaey as gotmo or alumani.
Kankanaey farmers of Benguet have worked wet rice on terraced fields for centuries.
The Kankanaey are one of the three major ethnolinguistic groups of Benguet province, with the Ibaloi and Kalanguya.

n.l: Benguet and Mountain Province in the Cordillera of northern Luzon, Philippines

f.t: Lumad advocacy, with allies, helped write two important provisions into the 1987 Philippine Constitution.
Lumad is a shared name for many Indigenous peoples of Mindanao, among them the Manobo, Subanon, Mandaya, Talandig and Teduray.

n.l: Mindanao, Philippines

f.t: Suri Jagek, meaning observing the sun, is the Kalasha system of reading the sun, moon, stars and shadows; UNESCO listed it for urgent safeguarding in 2018.
Kalasha families use Suri Jagek to choose the right time to sow seeds and care for livestock, and to anticipate natural hazards.

f.p: Press Information Department, Government of Pakistan
f.t: Suri Jagek is practiced at local observatories in three Kalasha valley villages: Bamburet, Birir and Rumbur.

n.l: The Kalasha valleys of Bamburet, Birir and Rumbur in the Hindu Kush, Chitral, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan

f.t: The Akha are one of more than 20 highland Indigenous peoples of northern Thailand.

n.l: Northern Thailand, eastern Myanmar and northern Laos

f.t: In the Atayal language, the word Atayal means people, real people, or kinspeople.
The Atayal live across the mountains of northern and central Taiwan, the widest spread of any Indigenous people on the island.
Weaving and facial tattoos are hallmarks of Atayal culture, which follows gaga, the teachings handed down by the ancestors.

n.l: Mountain areas of northern and central Taiwan, across New Taipei, Taoyuan, Hsinchu, Miaoli, Taichung, Nantou and Yilan

f.t: About 59,536 Bunun people were counted in January 2020, with homes in Nantou, Hualien, Taitung and Kaohsiung.
The Bunun live higher in the mountains than any other Indigenous people in Taiwan, mostly between 500 and 1,500 metres.

n.l: Both sides of the Central Mountain Range in Nantou, Hualien, Taitung and Kaohsiung, Taiwan

f.t: In 2014 the Hla'alua were officially recognized as a distinct people, becoming the 15th Indigenous people listed in Taiwan.
The Hla'alua are formed by four communities, Paiciana, Vilanganʉ, Talicia and Hlihlara, in Kaohsiung City.

n.l: Taoyuan and Namaxia districts, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan

f.t: The officially registered Kanakanavu population was 356 in January 2020.
On June 26, 2014, Taiwan's government recognized the Kanakanavu as an independent people, the 16th on the official list.
Some Kanakanavu people understand their name as people living in a forest of Taiwan giant bamboo.

n.l: Namaxia District, Kaohsiung City, Taiwan

f.t: The Kavalan population was about 1,492 in January 2020.
After a name rectification movement, the Kavalan were officially recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2002.
Kavalan weavers have kept alive a distinctive craft of weaving with banana fibre.

n.l: Yilan and the Hualien and Taitung coasts, Taiwan

f.t: About 102,730 Paiwan people were counted in January 2020, living in the southern mountains of Pingtung and Taitung.
The Ravar branch of the Paiwan is known for outstanding carving and pottery.
Paiwan culture is known for equal gender rights and a system in which the first-born child succeeds to the family line.

n.l: Southern Central Mountain Range across Pingtung and Taitung counties, Taiwan

f.t: In some Pangcah communities, each age class takes its name from a key event of its time, so one class name marks the computer era.
Their own name, Pangcah, means people and kinsmen. The name Amis came from neighbours in Taitung and was later adopted by scholars.

n.l: East of the Central Mountain Range in Hualien and Taitung counties, plus the Hengchun Peninsula, Taiwan

f.t: About 14,517 Pinuyumayan people were counted in January 2020, and many have moved from eastern Taiwan to cities, where they are active in many fields.
Taitung City and Beinan Township on the Taitung Plain are the heart of Pinuyumayan life today.

n.l: Taitung City and Beinan Township on the Taitung Plain, Taiwan

f.t: About 13,465 Rukai people were counted in January 2020, living in Kaohsiung, Pingtung and Taitung.
For the Rukai, the lily stands for purity and courage, and the right to wear lily ornaments sits at the heart of their culture.

n.l: Southern Central Mountain Range in Kaohsiung, Pingtung and Taitung, Taiwan

f.t: The Saisiyat population was 6,730 in January 2020.
The Saisiyat live in northwestern Taiwan, in Hsinchu County and Miaoli County on either side of Ngangihaw mountain.

n.l: Hsinchu and Miaoli counties in northwestern Taiwan

f.t: The Sakizaya population was about 985 in January 2020.
Through a cultural revival led by the community itself, the Sakizaya were recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2007.

n.l: Hualien Plain, the East Rift Valley and coast, Taiwan

f.t: About 10,452 Sediq people were counted in January 2020, mostly in the mountains of Nantou and Hualien.
Three subgroups make up the Sediq, each with its own group identity: Seediq Tgdaya, Sediq Toda and Sejiq Truku.
For Sediq people, Gaya, the body of rules passed down from the ancestors, guides the way they live.

n.l: Mountain areas of Nantou and Hualien in central Taiwan

f.t: The Tao, who live on Lanyu, also called Orchid Island, numbered 4,684 in January 2020.
In Tao migration history, the ancestors lived on the Batanes islands of the northern Philippines before settling on Lanyu.
The people call themselves Tao, meaning human, while Yami is the name used officially.

n.l: Lanyu (Orchid Island), Taitung County, Taiwan

f.t: Thao people live mainly in Ita Thao Village in Yuchi Township and in Dapinglin, Shuili Township, both in Nantou County. They numbered about 817 in January 2020.
Thao oral history tells of ancestors who followed a white deer to Sun Moon Lake and found a fertile place full of fish.

n.l: Ita Thao Village by Sun Moon Lake and Dapinglin, Nantou County, Taiwan

f.t: About 32,333 Truku people were counted in January 2020, mostly in Hualien County.
The Truku were officially recognized as one of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples in 2004.
Truku people value their weaving and face tattoo traditions and follow gaya, the daily life norms passed down from ancestors.

n.l: Xiulin, Wanrong and Zhuoxi townships in Hualien County, Taiwan

f.t: The Tsou population was 6,702 in January 2020.
The Tsou homeland centres on Alishan Township in Chiayi County, southwest of Yushan in central Taiwan.

n.l: Alishan Township in Chiayi County, plus Nantou and Kaohsiung, Taiwan
